clinicalPearls: A group of immunodeficiencies caused by mutations in RAC2, a haematopoietic small GTPase that regulates the actin cytoskeleton in neutrophils and lymphocytes

Dominant-negative mutations classically cause a neutrophil-function defect that resembles leucocyte adhesion deficiency, with poor wound healing, delayed cord separation, and severe bacterial infection despite a rising neutrophil count

Activating (gain-of-function) mutations instead drive a combined immunodeficiency with progressive T- and B-lymphopenia, sometimes detectable through newborn severe combined immunodeficiency screening
Neutrophils show impaired chemotaxis, superoxide generation, and degranulation, so abscesses form poorly and infections are hard to clear
Presentation is usually in infancy or early childhood with recurrent and invasive bacterial infections
Diagnosis integrates neutrophil-function testing and lymphocyte studies with confirmatory RAC2 genetic analysis, and the mutation class guides interpretation
Management includes antimicrobial prophylaxis and treatment of infection, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for severe combined phenotypes
reference.pathophysiology: RAC2 encodes a Rho-family small GTPase expressed almost exclusively in blood cells, where it cycles between active and inactive states to control actin-dependent processes and assembly of the neutrophil oxidase. In neutrophils, RAC2 signalling is needed for directed migration toward chemotactic signals, for the respiratory burst that generates microbicidal superoxide, and for granule release. Dominant-negative mutations block normal RAC2 activity, crippling neutrophil chemotaxis and killing so that bacteria are not cleared despite adequate cell numbers, mimicking a leucocyte adhesion defect. Activating mutations lock the GTPase in a constitutively signalling state that disturbs lymphocyte development and survival, producing progressive lymphopenia and a combined immunodeficiency. The net effect in either case is a serious predisposition to bacterial and, in the activating forms, broader infection.
additionalDifferentials: Typical severe combined immunodeficiency (for the activating phenotype)
Other cytoskeletal immune defects such as DOCK2 deficiency
Glycogen storage disease type Ib with neutrophil dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Neutrophil chemotaxis, oxidative burst, and degranulation assays
Full blood count with neutrophil counts over time
Lymphocyte subset enumeration and T-cell receptor excision circle quantification for combined phenotypes
Genetic sequencing of RAC2 with interpretation of mutation type
Adhesion-molecule expression studies to distinguish leucocyte adhesion deficiency
Microbiological cultures to guide antimicrobial therapy
redFlags: Severe bacterial infection with poor wound healing and delayed cord separation
Abscesses that fail to form pus despite high neutrophil counts
Progressive lymphopenia or an abnormal newborn screen in the activating phenotype
A family history of early infection consistent with a dominant or other inheritance pattern
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the mutation class and severity; the neutrophil-function defect can be life-threatening in infancy and the combined immunodeficiency of activating mutations is severe, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offering the prospect of cure when infections are controlled.
pitfalls: Confusing the neutrophil-function defect with leucocyte adhesion deficiency without genetic clarification
Reassurance based on a normal or high neutrophil count despite defective function
Overlooking progressive lymphopenia in activating mutations
Giving live vaccines before a combined defect is excluded
Delaying definitive treatment while recurrent infections accumulate
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
